title: Part 1 — Environment & tools
tagline: Set up a machine from scratch: terminal, VS Code, Node.js, Git and GitHub.
intro: Done once, used for the whole path. Type each command, read what it prints, and check it against the step before moving on.
Windows follows the WSL section, macOS the Command Line Tools section; from VS Code on, both do exactly the same.

blocks.caption: Each step needs the one before it.

items.label: How the web works
items.detail: The browser asks; a server answers with HTML, CSS and JavaScript
explain: Type shopee.vn: DNS turns the name into an IP address, the browser sends an HTTP request there, and the server's HTML is drawn on screen.
The frontend runs in the browser (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React). The backend runs on a server (Node, Express, MySQL). Full-stack does both.

items.label: Terminal
items.detail: Where commands run: npm, git and servers. Windows uses WSL, macOS its Terminal
explain: WSL runs a real Ubuntu inside Windows. That way every command in the videos and in this path runs the same as on macOS and Linux.
A prompt ending in $ is where you type. For example dong@laptop:~/code$ means user dong, in the folder ~/code.

items.label: VS Code
items.detail: The editor: it opens folders inside WSL and has its own terminal
explain: Type code . in a terminal to open the current folder in VS Code. On Windows, the WSL extension lets it edit files inside Ubuntu.
Prettier formats on save, ESLint flags JavaScript mistakes as you type, and Live Server reloads the page when HTML or CSS changes.

items.label: Node.js via nvm
items.detail: Runs JavaScript outside the browser and installs libraries with npm
explain: nvm manages Node versions: nvm install --lts installs the newest long-term support release, and nvm use 22 switches to 22 for an older project.
npm comes with Node. npm install express downloads the library into node_modules and records it in package.json so others can install it too.

items.label: Git & GitHub
items.detail: Git keeps code history on your machine; GitHub keeps a copy online
explain: Each commit is a snapshot of the whole project with a message. Break something and you go back to the previous commit, losing nothing.
An SSH key tells GitHub this machine is yours, so pushing needs no password. One key per machine.

items.label: First repo
items.detail: Make a folder, commit a README and push it to GitHub to test the whole chain
explain: The four daily commands: git status shows changes, git add picks files, git commit saves a snapshot, git push sends it to GitHub.
Seeing the README on the GitHub repo page means everything in this part works: terminal, Git, SSH and GitHub.

sections.title: How the web works
sections.summary: Five ideas you meet again in every later part.

items: Domain: a memorable name like f8.edu.vn instead of an IP address such as 104.21.3.10.
DNS: the Internet's phone book, turning a domain into an IP address.
Client and server: the browser (client) asks, and the server works out the answer.
HTTP: the language of requests and answers. GET fetches, POST sends new data, PUT changes it, DELETE removes it.
HTML, CSS, JavaScript: the three things a browser understands. HTML is content, CSS is looks, JavaScript is behaviour.

rows: A page or API returns data normally
A POST created a new record
Data is missing or wrong, such as an empty email
Calling a protected API without a token
A wrong path, or a record that does not exist
Backend code threw; read the log in the server's terminal

sections.title: Windows: install WSL
sections.summary: Ubuntu running inside Windows; skip this on a Mac.

items: Press Start, type PowerShell, right-click it and choose Run as administrator.
Run wsl --install below. It turns on WSL 2 and installs Ubuntu, taking 5–15 minutes.
Restart when asked.
Open Ubuntu from Start. The first time it asks for a Linux username and password: pick a short lowercase name, and remember the password, since sudo asks for it.
Update Ubuntu with the second command below. Typing the password shows nothing on screen: just type it and press Enter.
Install Windows Terminal from the Microsoft Store if missing, then make Ubuntu the default profile in Settings.

blocks.caption: In an administrator PowerShell. The second line checks: Ubuntu must show VERSION 2.
In the Ubuntu window: refresh the package list and upgrade.
code: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

body: Keep code in Ubuntu's home folder, such as ~/code, not under /mnt/c. npm running on the Windows drive through WSL is far slower.
Open the Ubuntu folder in File Explorer by typing explorer.exe . in the Ubuntu terminal.

sections.title: macOS: Command Line Tools and Homebrew
sections.summary: On a Mac the Terminal is built in; it only needs the command-line tools.

items: Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space, type Terminal, press Enter.
Run xcode-select --install and press Install in the dialog. It brings git, make and a compiler.
Install Homebrew with the second command. It ends by printing two Next steps commands: copy and run them to put brew on your PATH.
Check with brew --version and git --version: both printing a version means you are done.

blocks.caption: Command Line Tools, Homebrew, then a check.

sections.title: Terminal commands to know
sections.summary: Ten everyday commands, the same on Ubuntu and macOS.

rows: Lists files; ls -la includes hidden ones
Changes folder; cd .. goes up, cd ~ goes home
Makes a folder; -p makes parents too
Deletes for good, no trash; -r for folders
Clears the screen; Ctrl + C stops a running command

blocks.caption: Practice: type them in order and run ls after each to see the change.

body: Tab completes file and folder names, and the up arrow recalls the last command. These two keys save the most time.

sections.title: Install VS Code
sections.summary: One editor for the whole path.

items: Download VS Code from code.visualstudio.com and install it as usual. On Windows, keep the Add to PATH option.
Windows: install the WSL extension, then type code . in the Ubuntu terminal. The bottom-left corner showing WSL: Ubuntu means it worked.
macOS: open the Command Palette (Cmd + Shift + P) and run Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH so the code command works.
Install the extensions in the table below from the Extensions bar (Ctrl + Shift + X).
Open the JSON settings (Command Palette → Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)) and add the snippet below to format on save.

rows: Formats HTML, CSS and JavaScript on save
Flags JavaScript mistakes as you type
Opens HTML in the browser and reloads on save
Shows who changed each line, and when

blocks.caption: Add to settings.json, keeping the lines already there.

sections.title: Install Node.js with nvm
sections.summary: The same way on Ubuntu (WSL) and macOS.

items: Run the nvm installer (first line below). The latest release on 11 October 2026 is v0.40.8.
Close and reopen the terminal, or run source ~/.bashrc on Ubuntu and source ~/.zshrc on macOS.
Install the LTS release: nvm install --lts. It downloads Node 24 and makes it the default.
Check: node -v prints v24 followed by smaller numbers, and npm -v prints npm's version.

blocks.caption: Install nvm, reload the shell, install Node LTS and check. On macOS use ~/.zshrc instead of ~/.bashrc.

body: On 11 October 2026 the LTS is Node 24 (Krypton), supported until April 2028. Node 26 is due to become LTS in late October 2026; then run nvm install --lts again.
Windows: install Node inside Ubuntu as above, not the Windows build, so two different Nodes never get mixed up.

sections.title: Install and configure Git
sections.summary: Git writes your name on every commit, so configure it first.

items: Ubuntu (WSL): install Git with apt (first line). macOS: Git came with the Command Line Tools.
Set your name and email: use your GitHub account's email so commits show your avatar.
Make main the default branch and VS Code the editor Git opens.
Check with git config --list: the user.name and user.email you set must be there.

blocks.caption: Replace Your Name and you@example.com with your own.

sections.title: Connect to GitHub over SSH
sections.summary: Once per machine; after that pushing never asks for a password.

items: Create an account at github.com if you have none.
Create an SSH key with ssh-keygen. Press Enter to keep the default location; setting a passphrase is wise.
Start ssh-agent and add the key so the passphrase is not asked every time.
Print the public key with cat and copy the whole line.
On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, paste it and save.
Test with ssh -T git@github.com: type yes the first time; GitHub greeting you by username means success.

body: The "Set up SSH for git" guide on this site goes deeper: two GitHub accounts on one machine, and keeping the passphrase in the macOS Keychain.

sections.title: Your first repo
sections.summary: Test the whole chain: terminal, Git, SSH and GitHub.

items: On GitHub press New repository, name it hello-git, keep it Public, leave Add a README unticked, and press Create.
In the terminal make a folder of the same name and a README (first three lines below).
Initialise Git, add the file and commit.
Connect to the GitHub repo and push. Replace your-username with your GitHub username.
Reload the repo page on GitHub: seeing the README means done.

blocks.caption: From an empty folder to a repo on GitHub.

rows: See what changed and what is not added yet
Stage every change in the folder for the next commit
Save a snapshot with a short message saying what you did
Bring new commits from GitHub down
See the commit history, one line each
